question: Our squads get handed tiny tickets like "tweak this button". How do I describe how far up the ladder of responsibility a squad's remit reaches, from chores to an entire product?
text:
To describe how far up the ladder of responsibility a squad's remit reaches, the Org Topologies framework provides a visual model called the Scope of Work Mandate (the vertical axis of organizational design)[1].
This vertical axis tracks the boundary of problem-solving handed to a team, ranging from fine-grained chores at the bottom to full business/product ownership at the top[1][2]:
The Ladder of Work Mandate (Vertical Axis)
Tasks Focus (Chores & Tickets)
Scope: The squad receives narrow, fine-grained tasks matching specific expertise (e.g., "tweak this button", "design a wireframe", "write CSS")[2].
Dynamics: The squad operates as a Doing Archetype[3]. Members lack visibility into the whole picture, cannot create end-to-end customer value independently, and rely entirely on external planners and coordinators to define what needs to be built[2][3].
Capabilities Focus (Features & Sub-functions)
Scope: The squad owns a complete functional feature or capability within a product or service (e.g., search feature, checkout flow, or claims processing)[2].
Dynamics: While teams at this level have more autonomy over a component, they often operate in Delivering Archetypes (sometimes called a "Feature Factory")[3][4]. They optimize for predictable output within a narrow functional silo but still rely on external management for overall product direction[3][5].
Partial-Business Focus (Business Verticals / Sub-products)
Scope: The squad (or team-of-teams) owns a distinct vertical business line or service area (e.g., Uber Ride vs. Uber Eats)[6].
Dynamics: The squad takes direct responsibility for business outcomes and customer value within that vertical, collaborating across boundaries to drive commercial success or failure[6].
Whole-Business Focus (Entire Product / End-to-End)
Scope: Squads collaborate directly on whole-product problems and broad customer value without permanent internal sub-product barriers[7].
Dynamics: The squad functions as a Driving Archetype, where directing, doing, and delivering merge into a single cohesive unit that owns the overarching product roadmap and customer outcome[7][8][9].
Unbounded Focus
Scope: The highest level of responsibility, where teams have the mandate to explore undiscovered customer needs or pivot to entirely new markets (e.g., pivoting a product strategy based on user feedback)[7].
The Complementary Dimension: Scope of Skills Mandate
To successfully move up the vertical ladder, a squad also needs a broader Scope of Skills Mandate (the horizontal axis of Org Topologies)[1][10]:
Functional Units: Single-specialty groups relying on constant hand-offs[11].
Multi-Skill Teams: Cross-functional but incomplete, retaining dependencies on outside specialists[12].
End-to-End / Expanding Teams: Possess all required skills—and the mandate to learn new ones—to deliver complete value without external hand-offs[13].
Key Concepts to Frame the Remit Shift
Outputs vs. Outcomes: Squads handed tiny tickets are trapped in an output mindset (measuring how many tickets or features are completed)[14]. Elevating their remit shifts them to an outcome mindset (measuring customer impact, revenue, or problem resolution)[14].
Directing vs. Driving: When management writes detailed task specs and delegates chores, they act as Directing Archetypes while the squad acts as Doing Archetypes[3][15]. In an Adaptive Topology, those boundaries dissolve into Driving Archetypes, empowering squads to self-manage towards a long-term Product Goal rather than task lists[9][16][17].
Cascading Strategic Context: Frameworks like NCTs (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) or Lean Value Trees (Vision → Strategic Goals → Bets → Initiatives) bridge this gap by giving squads high-level strategic bets or outcome commitments, allowing the squad itself to decide which micro-tasks are necessary to achieve the goal[18][19][20].
🎯 Would you like to explore how to map your current squads onto an Org Topologies map or discuss practical steps (such as framing work around Product Goals) to elevate their remit?

1.chunk:
In economic terms, this axis represents the switching costs to  work on something different (decreasing from bottom to top),  and, therefore how easy it is for the whole organization to  switch direction, ideally driven by feedback, innovation,  competition, or strategic changes.
The larger the scope of work the units own, the closer they  are to holistically understanding and solving real problems.

2.chunk:
PARTIAL  BUSINESS
WHOLE  BUSINESS
From Bottom to top:
1. Tasks Focus: Units work on the narrowest scope of work. Example: A Sous-​Chef  preparing ingredients, or a visual designer sketching a wireframe. As input, they  receive fine-​grained tasks that match their expertise (“chop onions”, “design  graphic”). It’s an org design decision to limit their mandate, even though they may  be capable of learning and doing more.
2. Capabilities Focus: Units work on a full “capability” within a product or service.  Example: Insurance Claims-​Processing Group. For products, a capability is often  called a feature or function. For services, it’s also called a service element. The unit  name usually signals the capability: Surgical Team, Engine Team, Web Search Team,  and so on. Common consequences include silo thinking and local optimizations.

3.chunk:
Doing Archetypes
People working in this quadrant of doing archetypes cannot  independently see “the whole” and cannot create end-​to-​end  customer value. They need to rely on external planners and  coordinators (directing archetypes), and other doing-​archetype  units (other limited specialists) to deliver value. Example: The  Sous-​Chef in a restaurant who reports to the Head Chef and has  many tactical responsibilities. 
Delivering Archetypes
This quadrant of delivering archetypes represents work units  (people, groups, teams, AI agents) capable of delivering value but  only within a narrow scope of work. Because of that, these  archetypes become siloed and may deliver the ‘wrong’ value. They  lack the big picture and flexibility to change direction dramatically  and must rely on directive archetypes for value delivery. Example:  The Search Team in an E-​Commerce software platform.

4.chunk:
DIRECT﻿ING 
DOING
Resource Topology: Directing + Doing
Delivery Topology Compared to the Resource Topology, this topology upgrades  delivery units to have fast flow by removing dependencies.  Structurally, this typically involves forming complete cross-​ functional teams, and facilitating a smoother path to  “completely done” work. In some domains, this topology is  called a “Feature Factory” since Delivery units can provide a  near-​endless stream of features. Note a strong focus on  outputs and local efficiency.

5.chunk:
However, in order to streamline delivery, discovery must  remain separated in space and time. Similar to the Resource  Topology, Directing Archetypes emphasize up-​front analysis  to supply the work, and they may direct an “analysis Doing  unit” to discover and then write “the specs”, or they may  create them themselves. 
Keeping the teams ‘fast’ and constantly ‘efficient’ in  producing the outputs is only possible when the teams in the  Delivery Archetypes are permanently fixed to a narrow work  scope—​an internal component or a specific set of  capabilities. The other side of this coin is that they cannot  easily switch contexts. By the intentions of this org design,  teams lack the work mandate to engage with the “big  picture” but are allowed to expand their skill set becoming  more and more efficient within their narrow area of expertise.

6.chunk: 3. Partial-​Business Focus: Units work on a particular business vertical, clearly  separated from the other areas. Example: Uber Ride versus Uber Eats, two separate  profit centers within a single company. A key characteristic of partial-​business units  (e.g. all Teams within Uber Ride) is cross-​team collaboration and learning because  they are closely involved in business success or failure and so care about outcomes.  The need for close collaboration between teams at this level usually leads to  organizational simplification.

7.chunk:
4. Whole-​Business Focus: Units work and collaborate on whole-​business problems  and customer value. Example: Two-​person Instagram-​like startup. There is no  permanent separation inside the unit, such as business verticals, sub-​products, or  alike. At a larger scale, Teams may have a short-​term focus but are not stuck there.
5. Unbounded: This level refers to a state where units go where they want to explore  new ideas to satisfy undiscovered customer needs, possibly from unknown markets.  And they learn whatever they need. Example: A startup, such as a failing games  company who kept pivoting until they found a product that succeeded, in their  case, the collaboration tool Slack.

8.chunk:
Driving Archetypes
This is not ‘driving’ others. Imagine a car with passengers, any one of  whom can drive, who together decide where they want to go, drive and  arrive, and then go on. These driving archetypes are capable of  understanding, creating, and delivering customer value in its broadest  sense. That's where directing, doing, and delivering come together.  These archetypes can grasp the concept of business objectives or end-​ to-​end customer journeys and deliver upon them jointly thanks to an  overlapping, shared scope of work and a broad skills mandate. Example:  A three-​person startup or five teams within a Team-​of-​Teams.

9.chunk:
The boundaries between teams are structurally removed and  replaced by larger constructs—​such as a Team-​of-​Teams—​ where organizational units work closely together across the  entire business (“Uber”) or a partial business domain (“Uber  Eats”).
“Synchronicity of work” is a unique emergent quality of this  topology: in contrast to the other two topologies where the  Doing and Delivering archetypes own a narrow scope of work,  here in the Adaptive Topology, the Driving archetype allows all  parties to work in unison.

10.chunk:
Horizontal Dimension of Org Design: Skills Mandate The Horizontal Axis
The horizontal dimension represents the scope of skills mandate  that is given to an organizational unit. This corresponds to the  level of autonomy a unit has in delivering items of work. The more  rightward an organizational unit is on the map, the more that unit  can quickly deliver without dependencies, and so the better the  flow of value delivery.
To make a connection to the popular software development  approach Scrum, in that model, the horizontal axis is the  increasing completeness of the Definition of Done.

11.chunk:
Five Horizontal Levels
From left to right:
1. Functional Units are individuals and groups specializing in a functional area,  often resulting in the creation of functional groups (or departments). Example:  Movie Costume Department. To produce value, work needs to be specified and  handed over to each of the specific individuals who contribute partial steps to  the end-​to-​end solution. The hand-​offs and information scatter increase the  need for coordination, resulting in slow delivery and high process waste.

12.chunk: 2. Multi-​Skill Units (cross-​functional teams) provide more flow and  responsiveness than Functional Units. Example: Surgical Team of doctors and  nurses. Multi-​skill Units are incomplete, meaning they do not contain all the  skills required to deliver value end-​to-​end. They co-​exist with functional units  and other teams on whom they depend to deliver complete value. Example:  The Surgical Team relying on Post-​Op Care Team, and both together needed  for a complete service for the patient.

13.chunk:
3. End-​to-​End Units independently do everything to deliver complete value to  customers and thus have no dependencies. Example: Software Feature Team.  This results in much faster flow, more responsiveness, shorter and stronger  feedback cycles from customer to creator (since there are no middlemen), and  less process waste. That usually leads to happier workers and customers.
4. Expanding Units are end-​to-​end units with the mandate to acquire new  skills when needed. Example: Special-​Forces Military Team. Such teams need  to continuously learn when preparing for new missions. Expanding Units keep  learning whatever is needed to stay end-​to-​end capable over time.

14.chunk:
One consequence of an org design with complete archetypes is that they can become independently  operating silos. Whether that’s a virtue or vice depends.
Output versus Outcome Archetypes
There is a well-​known management principle of maximizing outcomes while minimizing outputs.
Outputs—​such as number of surgeries, amount of software features, number of completed design  documents, or percentage of closed insurance claims—​are relatively straightforward leading metrics.  However, more output does not mean more outcomes. In fact, more output usually means more cost or  investment, which can lower profit (an outcome). Investing to increase outcomes (healthy people, profit) is  justified; ‘investing’ to increase output is suspect.

15.chunk:
So, an archetype can be output or outcome-​oriented. For an organizational unit to deliver outcomes, it  needs to work in a higher-​level business context, as seen on the OT map.
Complete  Archetypes
Outcome Archetypes
Output Archetypes
Incomplete  Archetypes
Four Archetype Groups Directing Archetypes
This quadrant represents directing archetypes that oversee the  higher scope of work and lack the capabilities to create customer  value. They design, coordinate, and essentially speculate on the  value by making plans and writing specs to be handed off to other  archetypes that can turn concepts into cash. Example: The  Project Manager is responsible for planning and allocating  resources to meet a project’s deadline but does not participate in  the actual creation of value.

16.chunk:
DIRECTING
DELIVERING
Delivery Topology: Directing + Delivering
Adaptive Topology The Adaptive Topology merges “directing, doing, and  delivering” into one holistic unit within the Driving archetypes,  where humans, AI agents, and robots collaborate on complex  problems in an adaptive way, and the group explores and  drives themselves in their ‘car’. The goal of this topology is  adaptiveness (easy, cheap change based on learning) and  customer-​centricity to discover and deliver customer delight.

17.chunk:
Commitment: Product Goal
The Product Goal describes a future state of the product which can serve as a target for the Scrum Team
to plan against. The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to
define “what” will fulfill the Product Goal.
A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined
users or customers. A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.
The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one

It takes advantage of the visual work properties found in the Lean Portfolio and guides decisions and initiatives that tightly integrate with customer value and corporate vision, helping avoid initiatives that are time (and budget) wasting. howTo: >- The LVT follows a Top-Down framework: Vision > Strategic Goals > Bets > Initiatives.

19.chunk:
MSPOTs are a goal-setting framework that ladders down, from leadership to individuals in teams. Typically, leadership teams develop MSPOTs, and then share them with functional managers in a top-down way.
These targets unite around strategic vision whilst preserving autonomy in functional teams
* Five items cascade down, each informing the next one below it:
    * Mission: Company’s big-picture vision, and it rarely changes
    * Strategy: Explains how the company plans to achieve the mission
    * Plays: 4-5 big annual initiatives that are part of the strategy
    * Omissions: Projects that won’t be worked on according to the strategy
    * Targets: Measurable and realistic means to hold everyone accountable whyDo: >- MSPOTS are a great way to set product goals when you need to unite your team around a strategic vision but don’t want to be prescriptive. They are a great communication method, alongside being a framework.

20.chunk:
These can help when Product Teams are working on ambiguous initiatives and need more context
* Narrative: 1-2 sentence qualitative description of what the team want to achieve in Qtr (a wordier Objective)
* Commitments: 3-5 measurable goals that ‘pod’ commit to by a specific date (like Key Results)
* Tasks: Defining the work that needs to be done in order to achieve commitment. Can be changed in cycle. whyDo: NCTs aim to give more context around goals as to ‘why’ they were defined. This is done to provide the team with more motivation, as well as to encourage a more realistic goal-setting mindset. Which can be easily lost in a very laser-focused environment. howTo: >- T﻿he best way to write your NCTs is to follow the framework:
* Narrative: Write a 1-2 sentence qualitative description of what the team want to achieve in the quarter
* Commitments: Draft 3-5 measurable goals that ‘pod’ commit to by a specific date
* Tasks: Define the work that needs to be done in order to achieve commitment. This can be changed in the cycle.
